billion from $6.39 billion and the company said that excluding currency, revenue rose

wsj.summary_analysis: The Heard on the Street column reports that Philip Morris International beat analysts' second-quarter earnings estimates but cut its full-year guidance because of anticipated weakness in what it calls reduced-risk products, primarily its IQOS smokeless-tobacco technology, with a strong dollar also seen as a further headwind for a company that sells cigarettes only outside the U.S. The column recalls that the stock had already suffered its sharpest-ever post-results drop following first-quarter results a few months earlier, and that more than $60 billion in market value had been erased over the prior year. It argues that the nature of Philip Morris as an investment has changed: in 2012 the company paid about $12 billion, or nearly 10% of its market value, to shareholders via buybacks and dividends while investing a little over $1 billion, reflecting cigarettes as a mature, low-investment product, but over the trailing 12 months capital expenditures were 50% higher while cash returned to shareholders was barely half the 2012 level, reflecting heavier investment behind the reduced-risk pivot. A dividend increase announced the same day, the column says, "didn't do much to assuage fears" over the uncertain bet on reduced-risk products. It notes Philip Morris's global heated-tobacco market share is similar to that of its Philip Morris cigarette brand internationally (1.6%), and that the company faces competition from upstarts such as Juul Labs, the leading reduced-risk brand in the U.S.
wsj.why_moved: The article states the stock fell another 5% early Thursday morning, on top of what it describes as the stock's sharpest-ever post-results drop following the first-quarter report a few months earlier. It attributes this decline specifically to the cut in full-year guidance tied to anticipated weakness in IQOS and other reduced-risk products, along with the strong-dollar headwind, notwithstanding that the quarter's earnings had beaten analysts' estimates and that the company simultaneously announced a dividend increase, which the column says failed to offset investor concern over the reduced-risk product bet.

Philip Morris’s bet on heated tobacco is still stumbling, but more important is that the
risk of failure is high and competition fierce
By Spencer Jakab
July 19, 2018 at 11:29 am ET
A customer examines caps for Philip Morris International's IQOS smokeless tobacco devices last year. AKIO KON/
BLOOMBERG NEWS
Where there’s no smoke, there’s fire for Philip Morris International PM 0.74% .
The tobacco giant was once again done in by a product meant to one day replace
cigarettes. Although Philip Morris handily beat analysts’ earnings estimates for the
second quarter, the company cut full-year guidance due to anticipated weakness in
what it calls reduced-risk products, primarily its IQOS smokeless-tobacco technology.

Shareholders are justifiably worried. The stock had its sharpest ever post-results drop
following first-quarter results a few months ago and fell another 5% early Thursday
morning. More than $60 billion in market value has gone up in smoke in the past year.
The reason is that the nature of Philip Morris
as an investment has changed. While
cigarette smoking is under assault from
health authorities and faces ever-harsher
taxation, that didn’t mean it couldn’t be an
altogether pleasant decline. Back in 2012, for
example, the company paid some $12 billion,
or nearly 10% of its market value, to
shareholders via buybacks and dividends and
invested a little over $1 billion. Cigarettes, a
150-year-old product in terminal decline,
don’t require significant new investment.
But in the past 12 months, the company had
50% more in capital expenditures and
returned barely half as much cash as in 2012.
A dividend boost announced on Thursday didn’t do much to assuage fears over the
company’s uncertain bet on reduced-risk products.
Investors were optimistic about these products because they carry higher margins,
for now at least. But they also face scrutiny from some health authorities and, more
significantly for shareholders, tougher competition.

similar to that of its Philip Morris brand cigarettes, which has an international market
